questions.title: Under Minn. Stat. § 181.101, can an individual employee ever recover "average daily wage" penalties, or are those exclusively enforceable by the Commissioner?
questions.question_body: The panel holds that only the Commissioner can seek the average daily wage penalties under § 181.101(a), citing the statute’s text and Hull v. ConvergeOne. But § 181.171, subd. 1, also says an employer is liable for "compensatory damages and other appropriate relief," and for "the civil penalties or damages provided for in the section violated." Why doesn’t "other appropriate relief" allow a court to award those penalties to a private plaintiff? Is the court’s interpretive move essentially that § 181.101(a) itself cabins who may collect the penalties, and § 181.171 just channels remedies that are otherwise authorized in the violated section? How decisive is the contrast with §§ 181.13 and 181.14, where the Legislature expressly lets employees collect penalties directly?

questions.title: If the employer pays back wages and liquidated damages under the MFLSA, does a plaintiff still have Article III standing to seek civil penalties payable to the Commissioner?
questions.question_body: The court vacates and remands to determine jurisdiction, invoking Laidlaw’s discussion of civil penalties deterring ongoing violations. What facts must Cohen establish to maintain standing for MFLSA penalties when he personally won’t receive them? Is it enough to show an ongoing or likely-to-recur overtime policy to satisfy redressability, even though the money goes to the state? Who bears the burden under voluntary cessation (Laidlaw) to prove it’s "absolutely clear" the violation won’t recur, and what kind of evidentiary showing would meet that burden in the wage-and-hour context?

questions.title: What remedies are actually available to private plaintiffs for notice violations under the Minnesota Wage Theft Act, § 181.032(d)(4), (f)?
questions.question_body: The opinion affirms dismissal of Cohen’s MWTA notice claim largely because he stipulated he’d been paid all wages and didn’t identify penalty authority. Does § 181.032 create any private right to civil penalties for notice violations, or are remedies limited to wages, liquidated damages, and/or administrative enforcement? If penalties exist only via other provisions (e.g., § 177.27), how would a plaintiff properly plead and prove entitlement to them for a pure notice-change violation?

questions.title: Did Cohen waive his request for injunctive relief by changing the requested injunction at summary judgment instead of amending the complaint?
questions.question_body: The panel says the district court "understandably" didn’t consider Cohen’s new request to rescind the 2019 policy because new claims must be raised via Rule 15, not briefing. How strictly do Eighth Circuit courts police variance between pleaded injunctive relief and later-requested forms at summary judgment? Would an amendment be required if the new injunction targets the same alleged unlawful policy but specifies a different remedy? Is there any leeway under Rule 54(c) to award unpleaded injunctive relief if tried by consent or fully briefed?

questions.title: Does stipulating that all overtime wages and MFLSA liquidated damages are paid eliminate Cohen’s live case or controversy for penalties and injunctive relief?
questions.question_body: The parties stipulated that wages and MFLSA liquidated damages were fully paid, leaving only penalties and injunctive relief disputes. Does that stipulation extinguish his personal stake (injury-in-fact) such that claims for penalties or injunction require proof of ongoing policy impacts to avoid mootness? How does the court distinguish between standing at filing and mootness after payment, and what role does the Town of Chester requirement (standing for each form of relief) play here?

questions.title: Can a district court reach the merits on summary judgment without first resolving a serious question about mootness and Article III jurisdiction?
questions.question_body: Here, the Eighth Circuit vacates the summary-judgment ruling on the MFLSA penalties issue and remands for the district court to determine its jurisdiction first. Is it error for a district court to grant summary judgment on the merits when mootness remains unresolved, or is vacatur the standard corrective measure? Are there narrow circumstances where a court can assume jurisdiction to reach the merits (e.g., hypothetical jurisdiction) in the Eighth Circuit, or is that categorically prohibited?

questions.title: What happens to putative class claims when the defendant tenders full relief to the named plaintiff before class certification in a wage-and-hour case?
questions.question_body: Cohen filed on behalf of a putative class but stipulated he’d been paid his wages and MFLSA liquidated damages, and the parties agreed summary judgment could resolve the case entirely. Did this effectively moot any putative class claims pre-certification? Is there any Eighth Circuit "relation back" or inherently transitory exception that could preserve class issues here, or did the stipulation foreclose that path?

questions.title: What is the pathway for attorney’s fees, costs, and prejudgment interest when substantive wage claims are paid but penalty and mootness issues remain?
questions.question_body: Judge Kobes notes vacating the district court’s ruling as to attorney’s fees, costs, and prejudgment interest. Under MFLSA/MPWA/MWTA fee-shifting provisions, can a plaintiff be a "prevailing party" if the defendant pays wages and liquidated damages mid-litigation without judgment? If penalties are jurisdictionally barred or denied, does that affect fee eligibility for the earlier, now-satisfied wage components? How do Minnesota statutes and federal case law treat fees where relief is obtained via voluntary payment rather than a court order?
